title: Bead normal forms and subcomplex detection for coherent realization
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, ordinary nerves and the subset-poset coherent realization $\mathfrak C$ of [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching]. Let $K$ be any small simplicial set. In simplicial degree $r\geq0$, form the ordinary category with objects $K_0$ and morphisms from $x$ to $y$ the $r$-simplices of $\mathfrak C[K](x,y)$, with its levelwise composition. This category is free on the following directed graph. A generating arrow is a pair $(\sigma,T_\bullet)$ consisting of a nondegenerate simplex $\sigma:\Delta^m\to K$ with $m\geq1$ (nondegenerate means not in the image of a degeneracy operator) and a weakly increasing flag of subsets
$$\{0,m\}=T_0\subseteq T_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_r=\{0,\ldots,m\}.$$
Its endpoints are $\sigma(0)$ and $\sigma(m)$. Thus every morphism has a unique finite composable word of these generating arrows; an empty word is the identity. These generating arrows are called beads. A bead is a nondegenerate simplex of its mapping simplicial set exactly when its flag has no repetitions; its degeneracies repeat entries of the flag. The faces and all other simplicial operators are those induced from the subset-poset simplex model, followed by expression as the unique word of beads. In particular the bead presentation describes the given $\mathfrak C[K]$, not a replacement up to weak equivalence.

For a degreewise injective simplicial map $i:K\hookrightarrow L$, the induced functor $\mathfrak C[i]$ is injective on objects and on each mapping simplicial set. Its image in every degree is the free subcategory generated by precisely those beads whose nondegenerate simplex $\sigma$ belongs to $K$. Equivalently, a word in $\mathfrak C[L]$ belongs to $\mathfrak C[K]$ if and only if its endpoints belong to $i(K_0)$ and each of its bead simplices belongs to $K$ (identified with its image under $i$). In particular an empty word belongs to the image exactly when its vertex belongs to $i(K_0)$.

source.place: Definitions 5.1.1 and 5.1.4, Example 5.1.7, Lemma 5.1.9, Definition 5.1.11 and Proposition 5.1.12, printed pp.26–30 (PDF pp.26–30); read online. The weak-flag formulation includes degeneracies of the nondegenerate beads of Proposition 5.1.12. No Stacks tag states this simplicial-enriched result.

proof.text: The simplex-colimit definition in [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching] preserves small colimits. Indeed, for a target simplicial category $A$, let $F_A$ be the simplicial set whose $m$-simplices are enriched functors $\mathfrak C[\Delta^m]\to A$, with operators given by precomposition. By the colimit universal property, an enriched functor $\mathfrak C[S]\to A$ is exactly a compatible family of such functors for the simplices of $S$, hence exactly a simplicial map $S\to F_A$. Cocones on any diagram of $S$'s correspond under this bijection to cocones of their realizations. This proves the required colimit mapping-out property; the simplicial-category colimits exist by [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting]. We use the actual simplex cocones throughout.

source.place: Definition 5.1.8; expanded mapping-out argument for its simplex-colimit construction

proof.text: In $\mathfrak C[\Delta^m]_r$, a nonidentity arrow $i\to j$ is a chain $U_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_r$ of endpoint-containing subsets of $[i,j]$, by [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching]. List $U_0=\{a_0<\cdots<a_k\}$. The chain is the composite of the $k$ chains $U_b\cap[a_{h-1},a_h]$, for $1\leq h\leq k$: their union is $U_b$ in each degree $b$. Each factor has initial subset consisting of its two endpoints. Conversely any factorization into such factors has its junctions exactly at the elements of $U_0$, so these factors are unique. The identity case $i=j$ is the empty word. Consequently this ordinary category is free on the chains whose initial subset has just the two distinct endpoints; degeneracies repeat subsets and preserve these generators. The support of a generator is its last subset $U_r$.

Induct simultaneously on $n$ over all simplicial sets having no nondegenerate simplices above dimension $n$. The inductive assertion is the stated free word presentation, with the generator $(\sigma,T_\bullet)$ realized by the actual functor $\mathfrak C[\sigma]$ on its flag. For dimension zero this holds: [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells], applied to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow S$, expresses $S$ as a coproduct of vertex simplices. Step 1 takes it to the discrete category on $S_0$ in every degree. For the induction step the same cited boundary-cell statement expresses $S$ as the pushout attaching its nondegenerate $n$-simplices to its $(n-1)$-skeleton along $\partial\Delta^n$. Here the skeleton means the simplicial subset generated by simplices of dimension at most $n-1$. Nondegenerate labels of these subsets agree with those in $S$: if $z=s_iw$ in $S$ and $z$ is in a subset, then $w=d_i z$ is also in it. Step 1 carries the attaching square to a pushout of simplicial categories, and [lem-coef-simplicial-category-degreewise-colimits] computes it in each ordinary degree.

source.place: Lemmas 5.1.2 and 5.1.9 and Proposition 5.1.12; skeletal induction made explicit using the existing boundary-cell presentation

proof.text: For $n\geq1$, apply the induction hypothesis to $\partial\Delta^n$, whose nondegenerate simplices are exactly the strictly increasing vertex lists on proper nonempty subsets of $[n]$. Under the map to $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$, a generator supported on a face with vertex list $V$ is sent, by the subset-image formula of [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching], to its chain of subsets of $V$, regarded as subsets of $[n]$. Its initial subset consists of the two endpoints and its last subset is $V$. Thus distinct boundary generators have distinct image generators: the final subset recovers $V$, and the chain recovers the flag on that face. Conversely a generator in Step 2 is in this image precisely when its support $U_r$ is a proper subset of $[n]$. Therefore the boundary map is the inclusion of the free subcategory on those generators. Its complementary generators have endpoints $0,n$, initial subset $\{0,n\}$, and final subset $[n]$; these are exactly the weak flags specified in the item for this simplex dimension.

source.place: Examples 5.1.7 and 5.1.10(i), Definition 5.1.11; boundary computation inside the induction, without invoking the general subcomplex assertion

proof.text: Compute the degree-$r$ pushout from Step 3 using Step 4 and [lem-coef-simplicial-category-degreewise-colimits]. Its lower-dimensional category is free by the induction hypothesis. Freely adjoin to it the complementary generators of each attached $n$-simplex, with endpoints given by its vertex images. This free category has the pushout universal property: a functor from it to an ordinary category is uniquely an old functor and arbitrary images for the new generators. A compatible functor from each whole simplex has exactly the same data, since the images of its boundary generators are already prescribed by the old functor and its attaching map. These assignments are inverse and preserve the given cocones. Thus the degree-$r$ pushout is canonically this free category, with no new relation among old or new generators. Object identifications in attaching maps cause no difficulty: they merely allow loops and additional composable words. The new generators are indexed by the attached nondegenerate $n$-simplices and the flags of Step 4, proving the inductive assertion. This completes the bounded-dimensional induction, without assuming that simplex maps into $S$ are injective.

source.place: Lemmas 5.1.2 and 5.1.5, and Proposition 5.1.12; free-generator universal-property calculation of the attaching pushout

proof.text: For arbitrary small $K$, the boundary-cell presentation of [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells] gives $K$ as the sequential union of its skeleta. Steps 1 and [lem-coef-simplicial-category-degreewise-colimits] identify $\mathfrak C[K]_r$ with the corresponding sequential colimit of the free categories just computed. The transition maps keep each existing generator and adjoin the ones with the next simplex dimension. This colimit is free on their union: every finite word lies in one stage, and equality of two such words is already equality of their letter lists in a stage containing all their letters. Equivalently, assignments of images to the union of generators are exactly compatible assignments at every stage. This proves existence and uniqueness of every finite bead word, including the empty word, for the given $\mathfrak C[K]$.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.12; passage from skeleta to arbitrary small simplicial sets via sequential colimits

proof.text: The simplex cocone and [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching] show that applying $s_i$ to a bead repeats $T_i$, hence yields the bead with that repeated flag. A repeated adjacent pair can conversely be removed, giving a lower-degree bead whose $s_i$ is the original one. If a bead with a strictly increasing flag were $s_i(v)$ for any mapping simplex $v$, write $v$ as its unique bead word from Step 6. Degeneracy sends each letter to the bead with its repeated flag; thus the resulting word has the same number of letters. To equal one bead, $v$ must be one bead, whose repeated flag cannot equal the given strict flag. This proves the claimed nondegeneracy criterion; for degree zero no degeneracy into that degree exists.

source.place: Example 5.1.7 and Definition 5.1.1; weak flags, degeneracies, and the nondegeneracy clause of Proposition 5.1.12

proof.text: For any monotone operator $\theta:[q]\to[r]$, the operator on the image of a flag under the simplex cocone is the image of $T_{\theta(0)}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_{\theta(q)}$, by [lem-coef-pinched-cube-latching]. Express that image as its unique word from Step 6. Simplicial operators on a general word act on all its letters and then compose their resulting words, since enriched composition is simplicial. This proves the asserted operator description, including faces whose first subset gains junctions or whose last subset loses support. The colimit identifications in Steps 1 and 5 preserve the actual cocones, so these are equalities in the specified realization, not in a category merely weakly equivalent to it.

source.place: Definition 5.1.8 and Example 5.1.7; simplicial operators on the actual simplex-colimit realization

proof.text: Identify a degreewise injective $i:K\to L$ with its simplicial image. It sends nondegenerate simplices to nondegenerate simplices: if $i\sigma=s_j\tau$, then $\tau=d_j i\sigma=i(d_j\sigma)$, so injectivity implies $\sigma=s_jd_j\sigma$, a contradiction. Moreover, if a nondegenerate simplex of $L$ lies in the image, its unique preimage in $K$ is nondegenerate, because a degenerate preimage has degenerate image. On actual simplex cocones, $\mathfrak C[i]$ therefore sends $(\sigma,T_\bullet)$ to $(i\sigma,T_\bullet)$. It is injective on vertices and on these generator sets. The free word presentations then give injectivity on every degree of every mapping simplicial set. Their image is exactly the words with endpoints in $i(K_0)$ and with every letter labelled by a simplex in $i(K)$: a nonempty such word lifts uniquely letter by letter, and the empty word lifts exactly when its vertex lies in $i(K_0)$. This is the free subcategory on the indicated vertices and beads, and proves the corrected subcomplex-detection equivalence.

source.place: Lemma 5.1.9 and Proposition 5.1.12; explicit free-word image argument including empty words
